items.actClause: AN ACT to amend the tax law, in relation to exempting commercial fuel cell systems and electricity provided by such sources from the sales tax imposed by article 28 of the tax law and omitting such exemption from the taxes imposed pursuant to the authority of article 29 of the tax law, unless a locality elects otherwise; and to repeal subdivisions (n) and (p) of section 1210 of such law relating to tax exemptions imposed by resolution in cities having a population of one million or more persons
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER:S4753

TITLE OF BILL:  An act to amend the tax law, in relation to exempting
commercial fuel cell systems and electricity provided by such sources
from the sales tax imposed by article 28 of the tax law and omitting
such exemption from the taxes imposed pursuant to the authority of
article 29 of the tax law, unless a locality elects otherwise; and to
repeal subdivisions (n) and (p) of section 1210 of such law relating
to tax exemptions imposed by resolution in cities having a population
of one million or more persons

PURPOSE:  To provide a tax exemption for the retail sale or lease and
installation of commercial fuel cell electric generating equipment or
the sale of electricity generated by such equipment from state sales
and compensating use tax and granting school districts and
municipalities, including New York City, the option to provide such
exemption.

SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:  Adds a new subdivision (jj) to section 1115 of
the tax law to exempt the retail sale or lease and installation of
commercial fuel cell electric generating systems equipment and the
sale of electricity generated by such systems from the sales and use
taxes imposed by sections 1105 and 1110 of the tax law; defines the
term "fuel cell electricity generating systems equipment"; amends
sections 1210(a) and 1212(a) of the tax law to include tax exemptions
for commercial fuel cell electric generating equipment and grants
municipalities, including New York City, the authority to enact the
same exemption; amends section 1224 of the tax law to clarify that
where a county with one or more cities with a population of less than
one million elects to enact these tax exemptions for commercial fuel
cell systems equipment and electricity, a city within such county
shall have the prior right to impose tax on such exempt equipment
and/or electricity to the extent of one half of the maximum rates
authorized under section 1210(a) of the tax law, and conversely,
clarifies that where a city of less than one million has elected to
enact these tax exemptions, the county in which such city is located
shall have the prior right to impose tax on such exempt equipment
and/or electricity to the extent of one half of the maximum rates
authorized under section 1210(a) of the tax law.

JUSTIFICATION:  Fuel cell electric generating technology has many
advantages. Fuel cells commonly provide power to host facilities
during power outages, enhancing storm response, and allow critical
facilities to remain operational in such events. Fuel cells are
exceptionally efficient, they can stretch available supplies of fuel,
reduce energy costs and help reduce our dependence on foreign oil. The
scalability and resiliency of fuel cells makes them suitable for a
wide range of heat and power needs in homes, offices, and factories.
In addition, this technology has a low impact on the environment, with
near-silent operation and low emissions, making it suitable in
locations where combustion systems may not be appropriate. Also, fuel
cells may be used in conjunction with solar panels or wind farms to
produce electricity when renewable energy is unavailable. The fact
that fuel cells can run 24 hours a day makes them equal or superior in
some cases to renewable technologies in terms of the displacement of
conventional fossil fuel generation, leading to lower air pollution
emissions, including CO2.


For these reasons, fuel cells should be treated on par with solar
energy systems when determining eligibility for tax exemptions for the
retail sale, installation and electricity generated from commercial
fuel cell electric generating technologies. Eliminating all state
sales taxes, and providing local municipalities an option to eliminate
their portion as well, will: improve our economy, help us meet our
clean energy goals, stimulate commercial clean energy installations,
and create green collar jobs.

LEGISLATIVE HISTORY: New legislation.

FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:  Approximately $500,000 to the State.

LOCAL FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:  Depends on whether local governments grant
tax exemption.

EFFECTIVE DATE:  This act shall take effect December 1, 2015 and shall
apply in accordance with the applicable transitional provisions in
sections 1106 and 1217 of the tax law.

items.memoText:
VETO MESSAGE - No. 197

TO THE SENATE:

I am returning herewith, without my approval, the following bill:

Senate Bill Number 4753-A, entitled:

    "AN  ACT  to  amend the tax law, in relation to exempting commercial
      fuel cell systems and electricity provided by  such  sources  from
      the  sales  tax  imposed by article 28 of the tax law and omitting
      such exemption from the taxes imposed pursuant to the authority of
      article 29 of the tax law, unless a locality elects otherwise; and
      to repeal subdivisions (n) and (p) of section  1210  of  such  law
      relating  to tax exemptions imposed by resolution in cities having
      a population of one million or more persons"

    NOT APPROVED

  This bill would amend various provisions of the Tax Law to  provide  a
State  sales tax exemption on the retail sale, lease and installation of
commercial fuel cell electricity generating equipment  or  the  sale  of
electricity  by  such  equipment.  Localities and school districts would
have the option to offer such exemptions.

  Developing and using fuel cell electricity is  a  laudable  enterprise
and consistent with my efforts to promote and develop alternative sourc-
es  of  energy. New York State has a history of supporting the growth of
the fuel cell electricity industry and will continue to do so.  Further,
as  part  of  my  Reforming  the  Energy Vision initiative, I expect new
market opportunities for distributed generation  technologies,  such  as
fuel  cells, to provide greater value to customers and the central power
grid.

  Unfortunately, this bill contains  significant  technical  flaws,  and
would  be very challenging to implement as drafted. For example, certain
definitions in the bill condition exemptions on adherence to unspecified
standards, and in doing so, violates, Article III, Section 16 of the New
York State Constitution. Additionally, drafting errors in the bill  will
negatively impact New York City's existing solar energy credit. Separate
and apart from these flaws, providing tax exemptions for such activities
will  have  a revenue impact on the State and should be discussed in the
larger context of the upcoming State Budget.  Accordingly,  while  I  am
constrained to disapprove this bill for these reasons, I look forward to
working  with the bill's sponsors on how best to encourage the growth of
fuel cell technology in the State.

  I am further directing the New York State Energy Research and Develop-
ment Authority to continue to explore  opportunities  to  stimulate  the
growth  of  fuel  cell  electricity generation without subsidies, and to
coordinate its efforts with other State agencies.

  The bill is disapproved.                    (signed) ANDREW M. CUOMO
